title: Common causes for quantum identical particles
authors: A. Hovhannisyan, S. Weigert, A. E. Allahverdyan
abstract: Violations of Bell's inequalities imply that joint probabilities generated by non-commutative measurements on two (non-identical) quantum particles do not have a single common cause. But joint probabilities generated for such non-identical particles via commutative measurements do have non-trivial common cause variables. We focus on commutative measurements and consider two identical quantum particles, whose density matrices and observables (hermitian operators) are necessarily permutation-symmetric. It is natural to demand that the common cause describing joint probabilities is also permutation symmetric, i.e., it acts symmetrically on both particles. Looking at various ways of defining joint probabilities from the same measurement data, we conclude that either symmetric common causes need not exist (i.e., that the particles can be hiddenly distinguishable), or that symmetric screening variables exist, but they are trivial, i.e., no single common cause can explain all single-measurement correlations.
summary: This theoretical paper examines the Principle of Common Cause (PCC) applied to joint probabilities measured on two identical quantum particles. It finds that due to the required permutation symmetry of observables, a single common cause variable is either non-existent or trivial. This suggests that explaining all observed correlations requires assuming effective distinguishability between the particles.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether joint probabilities measured on two identical quantum particles can be explained by a single common cause, contrasting this with non-identical particles and addressing the constraints imposed by quantum mechanics.
main_result: The analysis concludes that either symmetric common causes do not necessarily exist (suggesting hidden distinguishability), or any existing symmetric screening variables are trivial, meaning no single common cause can explain all measured correlations.
method: It applies the Probabilistic Common Cause (PCC) framework to joint probabilities derived from measurements on identical particles, comparing results obtained by assuming particle labels versus using label-free event descriptions.
model_or_system: The system involves two identical quantum particles whose observables must be permutation-symmetric. The analysis uses projectors related to spatial and internal spin degrees of freedom within a tensor-product Hilbert space.
key_observables: Joint probabilities $p(A, B)$ derived from measurements; screening variables $C$ used in the common cause factorization.
important_parameters: The requirement for permutation symmetry on observables and the structure of the joint probability distributions.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is testing the applicability of the PCC framework to quantum correlations, particularly when restricted by particle indistinguishability (permutation symmetry).

paper_structure: The paper moves from discussing non-identical particles and Bell violations to focusing on identical particles. It compares labeled vs. event-based common cause approaches, ultimately concluding that the constraints imposed by quantum indistinguishability severely limit or eliminate the possibility of a single common cause variable.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles fundamental issues at the intersection of quantum foundations and causality (PCC), which is crucial for understanding how local hidden variables might manifest in multi-particle quantum systems, even when measurements are commutative.
